newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore leaders seek record damages for libel.
newsitem.headline: Singapore leaders seek record damages for libel.

text.p: Singapore's leaders asked a court on Wednesday to award a record S$12.9 million in damages against an opposition politician they said had tried to destroy their honour and reputations.

"Collectively, it would be the largest award of damages for libel in Singapore," a legal source said. The final bill could be considerably higher if the court awards costs against opposition politician Tang Liang Hong, he added.

Singapore's founding father, Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew, sought S$3.35 million (US$2.33 million) from Tang, who lost in January general elections and then fled to Malaysia saying he had received death threats.

Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong asked for S$2.15 million and Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong sought S$2.1 million from Tang, who was a major target of the long-ruling People's Action Party (PAP) during the election campaign.
Tang was sued by Goh, Lee and 10 other PAP leaders for calling them liars over their allegations he was an "anti-Christian Chinese chauvinist" who endangered racial harmony in Singapore.

"The case for substantial damages is compelling," Lee Kuan Yew's lawyer Davinder Singh told the court on Wednesday during a hearing to determine damages. The libel cases were awarded to the PAP leaders in March after Tang failed to turn up to defend himself.
"The concepts of truth and morality are alien to him," Singh said of Tang. "A ruling that excoriates the defendant will go a long way to vindicate (the PAP leaders)."
Singh said the damages should be awarded because Tang "perpetrated the libel and repeated it" after the elections by giving media interviews.
"When he was sued, he ran away," he declared.
In media interviews, Tang disdained assurances by Goh that he would not be arrested if he returned to Singapore, another reason he was sued for libel.
Tang, who fled to the south Malaysian state of Johor, said Goh's suggestion that he seek police protection was akin to a chicken seeking protection from a fox.
Singh said Tang should also be punished for drawing the attention of Malaysian media and officials to the comments by Lee Kuan Yew which seriously damaged relations between the two countries.
Lee had questioned in an affidavit why Tang would seek refuge in Johor, which he said was notorious for crime.
The statement outraged Malaysia, which demanded an apology and a retraction from Lee, who led Singapore as Prime Minister for 30 years until stepping down in 1990.
Lee apologised for the remarks and later received court approval for them to be stricken from the record.
Singh accused Tang of using the statement as "part of his political vendetta" against the PAP leaders.
Tang fired his lawyers on Monday, a move finally accepted by the court on Tuesday, saying he had wanted to be represented by a top London lawyer who was not available this week.
Lee told the court he believed Tang's move was in preparation for more interviews in which he could attack the Singapore judicial system. ($1 = S$1.44)
